title: Rising Rates Cleave AI Infrastructure Stocks (NASDAQ: CRWV, NBIS, MSFT, MU) Into Winners And Losers - Foreign Policy Journal
content: By Ewan Scott | Nov 8, 2026 | Economy & Business, Featured, News & Analysis A widening chasm has opened inside the AI infrastructure sector, and the dividing line is not technology but balance sheets and the cost of borrowed money. With the Federal Reserve holding its benchmark rate at 3.75% to 4.00% and markets pricing in a 72% chance of another quarter-point hike in December, debt-heavy data center builders are absorbing punishment that cash-rich rivals are largely avoiding. The numbers tell the story bluntly: CoreWeave (NASDAQ: CRWV) lost 47.54% of its market value in the single month ending November 6, while Nebius Group (NASDAQ: NBIS) shed 45.4% over the same stretch. Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT), which has not yet tapped the debt markets according to CFO Amy Hood, edged 0.16% higher across that same period, a near-perfect illustration of the divergence now reshaping the sector. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh captured the underlying dynamic during a late-October address, warning that “interest rates get in the cracks,” before adding that “interest rates affect directly or indirectly almost everything,” including the trillion-dollar AI buildout financed heavily with borrowed capital. Long-term borrowing costs are amplifying the Federal Reserve’s pressure from above, with the 10-year Treasury yield reaching 5.24% on October 9 and still sitting at 4.84% on November 5, the same day the VIX volatility index climbed to 28.18, its highest level since early August. CoreWeave’s financial structure illustrates the vulnerability most starkly, with debt running at 8.94 times equity and second-quarter interest expense hitting $640 million, more than double the $267 million recorded a year earlier. The company has guided for $860 million to $940 million in third-quarter interest expense alone, even as it plans to deploy $35 billion to $39 billion in capital spending this year against a revenue backlog of $104.2 billion. Nebius faces a comparable squeeze, having sold $4.34 billion in convertible notes during the first half of the year to help finance $20 billion to $25 billion in planned capital expenditure, with three customers accounting for 24%, 21%, and 14% of its second-quarter revenue, concentrating risk dangerously. Oracle (NYSE: ORCL) sits on $664 billion in signed future revenue but burned $5.4 billion in free cash flow last quarter while capex hit $28.5 billion and interest expense surged 55%, prompting CFO Hilary Maxson to acknowledge that the company has “not given a particular time frame on that yet” for when free cash flow turns positive, as the stock falls 39.64% for the year. Microsoft’s $18.6 billion in quarterly free cash flow, generated even after $45.2 billion in capital spending, positions it as the clearest beneficiary of the current environment, while Alphabet moves in the opposite direction, recording negative $9.07 billion in free cash flow after $51.36 billion in capex and raising $28.7 billion through new bond issuance. Even companies with strong cash generation are not immune, as Micron Technology (NASDAQ: MU) demonstrates, with its stock dropping 36.57% over the past month despite producing $62.3 billion in free cash flow during fiscal 2026. Micron’s exposure stems from its customers, specifically the high-bandwidth memory buyers who are the same debt-dependent data center operators now facing tighter financing conditions, meaning demand for Micron’s chips could soften even without any chip-supply problem. Investors watching for early signals of stress should focus on CoreWeave’s upcoming third-quarter earnings report, where interest expense at or above the top of guidance would confirm that borrowing costs are already constraining the company’s growth trajectory. The Federal Reserve’s December meeting then becomes the next critical inflection point, since another rate increase would raise financing costs on data center contracts structured when capital was substantially cheaper than it is today. Ewan is a reporter at the Foreign Policy Journal, primarily covering US current affairs and news related to NYSE-listed stocks. He has over two decades of experience in journalism and digital publishing.

title: Berkshire Earnings Drop As Market Seeks Repair, Sandisk And Micron Crumble While Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL), Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN) And Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) Hold Firm - Foreign Policy Journal
content: By David Prior | Nov 8, 2026 | Economy & Business, Featured, News & Analysis Berkshire Hathaway (NYSE: BRK-B) reported a decline in earnings, adding fresh pressure to an equity market already struggling to find stable footing heading into the new trading week. The broader market is in a damaged state, with investors navigating a landscape where former high-performing names have lost significant ground and the path to recovery remains unclear. Dow Jones futures are set to draw close attention from traders on Monday morning after the index shed 0.46% in recent sessions, signaling continued unease across blue-chip holdings. Among the hardest-hit names, Sandisk and Micron have emerged as cautionary examples, with analysts characterizing both stocks as broken rather than merely pulled back from highs. The semiconductor and storage sectors have faced particular scrutiny, as the deterioration in Sandisk and Micron reflects broader concerns about demand cycles and inventory pressures weighing on the industry. Not every corner of the market is in retreat, however, with several mega-cap technology names demonstrating a resilience that stands in contrast to the broader selling pressure. Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL), which slipped just 0.44%, has managed to hold its ground relative to more battered peers, a sign that investor confidence in the consumer electronics giant remains comparatively intact. Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN) also showed relative strength with a modest decline of 0.14%, suggesting that its diversified revenue streams across retail and cloud computing continue to attract defensive positioning from institutional buyers. Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) dipped 0.85% but is still considered among the names holding up, as its enterprise software and artificial intelligence investments provide a degree of earnings visibility that the market continues to value. The divergence between resilient mega-caps and broken growth names underscores a broader rotation dynamic, where investors are gravitating toward companies with durable cash flows and retreating from those with shakier demand outlooks. Berkshire’s earnings decline is particularly notable given Warren Buffett’s conglomerate is often viewed as a bellwether for Main Street economic conditions, and weakness there may signal softening activity beyond just technology and semiconductors. With the market in need of repair and several key charts compromised, the coming week’s trading session will be critical in determining whether buyers are willing to step in or whether further deterioration lies ahead. David Prior is a senior reporter at the Foreign Policy Journal, covering everything from current affairs and global politics to stock market news and analysis.

content: By David Prior | Nov 7, 2026 | Economy & Business, Featured, News & Analysis Berkshire Hathaway’s earnings declined in the latest reporting period, adding pressure to an already fragile broader market that analysts say is in need of meaningful repair. The conglomerate’s profit drop stands in contrast to the relative resilience shown by three of the market’s most closely watched technology names heading into the weekend session. Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL), Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN), and Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) have each managed to hold their ground, offering investors some reassurance amid a generally unsettled trading environment. Microsoft slipped 0.85% and Apple edged down 0.44%, but both stocks are broadly considered to be weathering current conditions better than much of the rest of the market. The Dow Jones Industrial Average futures pointed lower, with the index off 0.46%, underscoring the cautious tone that has defined recent sessions. While large-cap technology is providing a degree of stability, conditions in the semiconductor space tell a sharply different story, with Micron (NASDAQ: MU) and SanDisk (NASDAQ: SNDK) both described as appearing technically broken. Despite that characterization, Micron actually gained 5.85% and SanDisk rose 4.34% in recent trading, though those moves have done little to alter the underlying technical damage both stocks have sustained. The divergence between short-term price pops and deteriorating chart structures in chip stocks reflects a broader tension running through the current market, where individual sessions can mislead about the health of a trend. Analysts tracking market internals have flagged the need for a sustained period of constructive price action before the broader indexes can be considered to be on solid footing again. The combination of weakening earnings from a bellwether like Berkshire, a shaky technical backdrop for semiconductor names, and index-level softness suggests the path to recovery will require patience from investors rather than a quick rebound. With large-cap technology stocks serving as one of the few dependable pillars of support, the market’s near-term direction may hinge heavily on whether Apple, Amazon, and Microsoft can maintain their current levels through continued volatility. title: Why The Blue Tsunami Rattled AI Stocks - Investor's Business Daily
content:
BREAKING: Futures Rise; Nvidia Probes CEO Huang Spying Case The trillion-dollar AI data center boom will likely face even greater scrutiny after Democrats won control over Congress and governors' mansions in several key states. The results have shaken AI stocks, highlighted by the past week's volatile trading. The Nasdaq tumbled sharply Thursday, before bouncing back Friday. Top AI stocks are set to close the week lower while the cloud giants also had a wild ride, with volatile trading for Amazon (AMZN), Microsoft (MSFT) and Google parent Alphabet (GOOGL).  The action underscores the challenges ahead for the AI megatrend after a Blue Tsunami election. Backlash to data centers — which act as the engines powering AI technology — has led to calls for moratoriums, bans and other legislation. The results in Texas were particularly striking. Ed Mills, the Washington D.C. policy analyst for Raymond James, said what happened in the Lone Star state, where Democrat Gina Hinojosa beat Republican incumbent Greg Abbott, could prove most impactful for AI stocks. Risk Management: How Invested In The Market Should You Be Right Now? "To use a different storm analogy, this is arguably a category five hurricane that hit the data center trade," Mills told Investor's Business Daily. "You have a candidate that has won, who said that the old moratorium was a scam and that, if elected, she would put in place a real moratorium. Now that's just Texas, but you also have a similar thing in Ohio." Hinojosa made opposition to data centers a key part of her winning campaign for Texas governor. She called for a broader moratorium on data centers until new legislation is passed. She was critical of a freeze Abbott placed on permits earlier this year. Additionally, she argues he would lift it following the election. Texas trails only Virginia for total data centers active or in the works, according to estimates from Pew Research. It is also the site of massive data center efforts such as the Abilene Stargate campus. Amy Acton in Ohio and Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia also made data centers a campaign issue. Following the midterms, research firm Cleanview found 41% of the current U.S. data center pipeline is located in states that have a governor or governor-elect pledging restrictions on the facilities. Data center backlash will bring challenges to Amazon, Microsoft and Google. The tech giants are the three leading cloud-computing providers. Each so-called cloud hyperscaler is spending hundreds of billions to build new data centers to meet demand. But the stock reactions following the midterms point to a more nuanced picture. Amazon, Microsoft and Google actually rallied on Wednesday. Then they pulled back sharply with the rest of the AI trade Thursday. On the one hand, restrictions on new data centers likely provide an edge to the biggest, most established cloud computing providers. Hyperscalers are the AI incumbents, as Needham analyst Laura Martin wrote to clients following the midterms. "We believe higher regulatory barriers entrench incumbents, and increase risks (and raise required ROICs) for new entrants," Martin wrote, referring to return on invested capital. Investors may not be all that upset if AI spending is forced to slow. Soaring capital costs have eaten the free-cash-flow of even tech's biggest players, raising concern on Wall Street in the lead-up to the elections. Some tech investors will view the midterms as a "slight positive" if the results force Big Tech to "hit the slow down button" on capital spending, Yorkville Ives analyst Dan Ives wrote on Wednesday. At the same time, AI demand has helped accelerate revenue growth for each of the three leading cloud businesses. Restrictions on data centers risk either raising costs or making it more difficult to meet demand. Meta Platforms (META) President Dina Powell McCormick said at a Wall Street Journal conference on Wednesday that building data centers in the U.S. is "going to be harder" following the midterm results. Tech companies may look to international markets, she added. While it doesn't operate an enterprise cloud infrastructure business, Meta is spending hundreds of billions on data centers to support its AI ambitions and massive portfolio of social media apps. The midterms fallout was also pronounced for companies that provide components used for the AI buildout, from chips and computer hardware to energy and construction. Nvidia (NVDA) stock fell sharply Thursday, its worst day since it tumbled after the release of Chinese AI model DeepSeek in January 2025. Nvidia also bounced back Friday, but was on track for a weekly loss. Other leading AI players also had a volatile week. Shares of Seagate (STX), Dell (DELL), Micron (MU) and CoreWeave (CRWV) were also poised to end the week in the red. Analysts with UBS estimate that data center pauses or moratoriums could put about 30% of the capacity previous expected in 2028 at risk. "The slowdown is a negative for Semis and AI infrastructure, but a lot is already priced into semis with valuations nearing multiyear lows," UBS strategist Keith Parker wrote in a client research note Wednesday. SpaceX (SPCX) is also a major developer of cloud infrastructure and AI.  Shares fell 4% Wednesday and 9% Thursday before regaining some ground Friday. Investors are also likely bracing for blowback from Elon Musk's big donations to Republican politicians. Investors are likely still sizing up the broader impact for AI stocks. Evercore ISI analyst Amit Daryanani said in a client note that increased scarcity could drive up prices for AI compute. Amazon, Google and Microsoft are poised to close the week higher. Amazon offered a bullish signal Wednesday by breaking a recent downward trendline drawn from a record high reached on Aug. 3. That was followed by a pullback Thursday and slight gain Friday. Microsoft jumped up from a test of its 50-day moving average Wednesday before easing back by 3.5% Thursday. Microsoft is the top-rated among the hyperscaler stocks with a best-possible 99 IBD Composite Rating, according to IBD Stock Checkup. The score combines five separate proprietary ratings into one rating. The best growth stocks have a Composite Rating of 90 or better. Google stock is still trading near recent lows that followed its Q3 earnings, despite the gains Wednesday. Nvidia is sharply below its 200-day moving average with the postelection tumble. Meanwhile, Raymond James' Mills said the backlash to data centers is tied to factors that extend well beyond the structures themselves. They have also come to represent concerns about AI's impact on jobs and even national security. "In a lot of these conversations, you see as much as 75% of the American people opposed to data centers," Mills said. "And it's not just because of affordability. It's not just because of environmental issues. It is the physical manifestation related to a lot of anxieties all wrapped up into one." That could make both data centers and AI fertile ground for politicians to run against in future elections. (Bloomberg) -- Microsoft Corp. is winding down an arrangement to rent AI computing from Oracle Corp., part of a larger reassessment of billions of dollars in cloud partnerships. Rubio Weighs Leaving Administration After GOP's Midterm Loss Morgan Stanley Offers $2.3 Billion Debt for Dell Family Deal Hinojosa Seeks 'Balance' With Musk, Regulations in Blue Texas Democrats Clinch Huge Wins on Inflation Anger, Trump Fatigue S&P 500 Sinks 4% as AI Washout Rattles Wall Street: Markets Wrap In recent months, Microsoft has been turning off rented computing capacity from Oracle after declining to renew the contract, according to people familiar with the matter. Over time, the computing Microsoft was renting became less useful because it no longer fit the company's specifications, said the people, who requested anonymity to discuss a private matter. The Oracle hardware used older-generation Nvidia Corp. chips, the people said. An Oracle spokesperson said demand for the company's AI infrastructure remains strong, including for earlier-generation graphics processing units. Oracle said in September that it was renewing contracts for four-year-old GPUs at a 20% premium to the original deal price. Under the arrangement, announced in 2023, Oracle agreed to sell Microsoft access to servers that would power a new AI-assisted version of the Bing search engine. The full size of the deal couldn't be determined. The fact that Microsoft was prepared to rent servers from a major rival was seen as an early indication of the massive shortage of processing power that has come to define the AI era. The world's largest software maker helped usher in a "neocloud" boom by signing massive contracts with upstart cloud businesses like CoreWeave, Nscale and Nebius. In all, Microsoft committed more than $80 billion to rent capacity from other cloud companies to bolster its own AI efforts. But Microsoft has been re-thinking its strategy. Key leaders at the company have grown frustrated with the neocloud providers over high costs and delays. In recent months, the company has tightened oversight of data center projects, stepped away from ones it deems risky and debated internally whether to ink new neocloud deals, Bloomberg previously reported. Oracle's cloud businesses has expanded rapidly since 2023, fueled by big AI contracts with companies like OpenAI and Meta Platforms Inc. For the year that ended in May 2026, Oracle's cloud business posted $18 billion in revenue. With Oracle developing data centers and expanding its cloud business, the company was initially seen as a major beneficiary of the AI boom. But investors have recently become concerned about heavy capital spending that has turned Oracle's free cash flow negative. The shares have lost more than half their value since hitting a high this year of $248.15 on June 1. title: The AI infrastructure boom faces a "global crackdown": restrictions on construction are crossing the Atlantic, with Microsoft's (MSFT.US) Amsterdam project at the eye of the storm. - 富途牛牛
content: The wave of restrictions on AI data center construction, triggered by the U.S. midterm elections, is spreading across the Atlantic to Europe. The wave of restrictions on AI data center construction triggered by the U.S. midterm elections is spreading across the Atlantic to Europe. Zhitong Finance APP has learned that on Friday local time, a group of protesters broke into a Microsoft (MSFT.US) data center construction site in Amsterdam, kicking off a two-day rally. This is part of a growing global backlash against the rapid expansion of computing power required for AI. According to the "Stop Dirty Data Centres" coalition, activist groups have announced actions in 16 countries on Friday and Saturday. The coalition brings together environmental organizations and digital rights movements to jointly call for a moratorium on large-scale construction. Reportedly, over 100 activists gathered at a Microsoft AI data center construction site in Amsterdam on Friday. They marched arm-in-arm, then breached the site, climbed construction cranes, hung balloons, and danced inside while police monitored from the sidelines. Some demonstrators held signs reading: "Tear down your data centers." The site owner, Pure Data Centres, plans to invest over $1 billion, with backing from Oaktree Capital, a subsidiary of Brookfield. The company stated it is committed to engaging with local stakeholders. "We urge those on-site to evacuate safely and engage in dialogue with us regarding this project and the concerns raised," the company said. Other planned protests include marches in Dublin, demonstrations outside the parliament building in Warsaw, and another protest targeting a Microsoft data center in Denmark. Microsoft stated that it understands the strong public opinions surrounding the project and respects the right to peaceful expression, but does not support any illegal activities. Tech stocks face sell-off amid market concerns over tightening AI regulation From Spain to India and the United States, resistance is gaining momentum. Driven by market fears that Democratic control of Congress could lead to stricter regulations stifling the AI boom, U.S. tech stocks fell sharply on Thursday. Senator Bernie Sanders' earlier proposal for a "national moratorium on new data centers," combined with the explicit commitment by the governor-elect of Texas—one of the most important hubs for AI data centers in the U.S.—to pause approvals for new projects, jointly triggered this "reckoning-style" sell-off across the AI supply chain. Protesters argue that data centers exacerbate strains on electricity and water resources, compete with housing and other industries for scarce resources, and hinder the achievement of climate goals. They also highlight risks of job losses, the concentration of computing power in the hands of large tech companies, and potential threats to personal and national security. Tech companies responded that data centers are the core infrastructure for meeting global demand for AI and cloud computing, serving as critical facilities for enterprises, governments, and general consumers. The “Stop Dirty Data Centres” coalition emphasized that it does not oppose technological progress nor call for the shutdown of existing data centers; rather, it advocates pausing new large-scale projects until clear regulatory frameworks are established in respective countries. In response, Europe faces internal contradictions: on one hand, it seeks to catch up with AI development in the United States and Asia to boost productivity; on the other, it aims to maintain relatively strict regulatory and public protection mechanisms. Henna Virkkunen, the EU’s top digital official, stated in an interview on Thursday that Europe needs more data centers to support AI development, but construction must proceed prudently. “AI is undoubtedly a crucial technology, and we must possess sovereign computing capabilities.” Virkkunen noted that Europe is ramping up chip manufacturing and investment in AI startups, with plans to establish a number of large-scale computing facilities within the region. However, she added, “For the public, one point is crucial: people must be assured that electricity bills will not skyrocket due to data centers, that power outages will not be triggered by computing infrastructure, and that such projects must not harm the environment.” It is reported that Google’s (GOOGL.US) project in Finland has been subject to a criminal investigation over land-clearing issues; Italy and Portugal are tightening environmental regulations for data centers; and Microsoft previously withdrew from a data center project in the UK due to delays in infrastructure development. title: What Are Microsoft Investors Betting On? - Trefis
content: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com. Microsoft (MSFT) stock trades at 26.8 times its adjusted earnings over the last twelve months. This profit figure leaves out one-time items and adds back stock-based pay after tax. That is a lot to pay for a single year of profit, and the multiple is about the same, 26.7 times, against the profit analysts expect for fiscal 2027. That forecast may not add back stock-based pay, so it may count profit on a different basis. The stock only looks cheaper against fiscal 2028 profit. So what kind of growth are you paying for at today’s price? The consensus forecast projects Microsoft’s revenue rising about 19% in fiscal 2027, to $395 billion. For fiscal 2028, the forecast anticipates sales growth of 20.5% and net income growth of 20.9%. The forecast’s net margin is 37.7% in fiscal 2027 and 37.8% in fiscal 2028. This means the profit growth you are betting on comes from more sales, not from wider margins. Based on the consensus forecast, Microsoft stock trades at 26.7 times fiscal 2027 earnings and 22.1 times fiscal 2028 earnings. Its trailing multiple on adjusted earnings is 26.8 times. Has Microsoft Delivered Sales Growth Near The Forecast? For fiscal 2027, Microsoft is close. Revenue grew 18.8% in fiscal Q1 2027, and management guided for growth of 18% to 19% in fiscal Q2. Over the last twelve months, though, revenue grew 17.9%. This means the fiscal 2028 forecast expects faster sales growth than Microsoft has delivered. That growth is uneven across the business. In fiscal 2026, Microsoft’s Intelligent Cloud segment grew 29.7%, while its More Personal Computing segment shrank 1.1%. Microsoft reported a net margin of 40.3% in fiscal 2026. The consensus forecast has a lower margin in both coming years. The forecast does not specify whether its profit is reported or adjusted, meaning the two margins may not be measured the same way. The likeliest place is data center capacity. On its October 28 call, management said customer demand continues to exceed available supply, and some third-party GPU capacity Microsoft was counting on for fiscal Q2 has moved into the second half of the fiscal year. Management guided for Azure growth of 49% to 50% in fiscal Q2 and said Microsoft needs further efficiency gains across its fleet to reach it. Any further delay would leave Microsoft less to sell and pull the sales forecast down. Microsoft has worked around these delays once already: Azure revenue grew 48% in fiscal Q1 2027, ahead of management’s expectations, even with third-party capacity arriving late. Price is the other place the forecast could slip. Management said the price Microsoft gets per token, a unit of AI work, can change through the quarter. Foundry, its platform for building AI agents, more than tripled its revenue from a year earlier in fiscal Q1 2027. Management named higher revenue per token as one reason Foundry beat expectations. A fall in that price would pull the sales forecast down too. If Microsoft delivers the consensus forecast, the multiples on fiscal 2027 and fiscal 2028 earnings are a fair picture of what you pay for the stock. If capacity arrives late or token prices slip, profit could fall short of the forecast. Those multiples would then understate what you pay, making the stock a riskier bet. Azure growth against management’s guide is the number to watch, and Microsoft is expected to report it in January 2027. Forecasts can slip, and so can markets. Build a portfolio that holds up either way. After a run like this, the hard questions are personal: hold, trim or sell, and the tax on each.
